changedBeliefs: The `select() round-trip floor` has been the terminal argument in this direction for months and was never a measurement. Claim 258.2 rejected a columnar result store partly because its sub-threshold transfer saving was `below the round-trip floor`; exp 264 put a point read at `5-8 us, most of which is the isolate round trip`; exps 209 and 239 both went after the floor by amortising a hop across several queries. It is now priced: on the canonical 6-column point read the hop is 6.3 us of an 8.4 us read, and removing it leaves 2.1 us. So the floor was real, it was most of a small read, and it is not a floor — it is a routing decision. Everything previously rejected as `below the round-trip floor` was measured against a denominator four times larger than the work it was competing with. This survives the candidate's rejection and is the run's lasting contribution.

Rows returned cannot bound main-isolate work, and this is why the candidate was rejected rather than shipped. It fails along three independent axes, each sufficient on its own. (1) One row can be arbitrarily large: `SELECT * FROM photos WHERE id = ?` has a permanent high-water mark of 1, is admitted forever, and — because there is no hop — has exp 236's blob wrapping suppressed, so a 5 MB image is copied straight onto the calling isolate. Cost also varies per *execution* of the same statement (id=1 a thumbnail, id=2 a raw), so no per-SQL history predicts the next parameter. (2) Rows returned is not query cost: `count(*)` over a large table and an unindexed `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10` both return few rows after unbounded work, and a result-shape signal is blind to work that happens before the first row. (3) Inline reads never yield, so N of them coalesce into one uninterruptible block rather than N interleavable ones. Any future routing policy must treat row count as an efficiency hint and never as a safety bound.

A guard set derived from the lanes you already have tests the hypothesis you already believe. Exp 265's nine lanes were all small integers and short TEXT, cheap indexed lookups, hot page cache — and every kill condition tested whether the *hint* was wrong about row count, which is the one failure mode the row cap already handled. The three real failure modes needed lanes that did not exist and that nobody would build while the happy path was reading -75%. The discriminating lanes are cheap and specific: a one-row read of a 5 MB blob, a `count(*)` over a large table, and a frame-shaped workload rather than a throughput one.

A safety property must be enforced, not predicted, and exp 265 contains one of each so the contrast is exact. The row cap predicts nothing — it aborts mid-decode and falls back, and it is correct whether or not the hint was right (+24.7% once per statement, claim 265.4). The eligibility test predicts, and every one of its failure modes is unbounded. The fix is two more enforcement points rather than a better predictor: `sqlite3_column_bytes` gives a cell's size before anything is copied into Dart (and the value is already loaded at the line where the wrap branch is skipped), and `sqlite3_progress_handler` interrupts every N VM steps. With both, the high-water hint stops being load-bearing and becomes what it is good at — avoiding wasted aborts.

The cost of the hop is not only its own latency but the queue in front of it, and no transfer-shaped analysis in this direction could see that. Exps 244/245/246 measured intrinsic transfer with a prepared-result barrier and pool capacity with a burst, both correctly, and both hold the *request* constant. A point read issued while four 1,000-row reads occupy every worker waits 533-1169 us against 37-52 us for one that never enters the queue. When the next runner asks what a scheduling change is worth, the lane has to contend for the pool; a lane that has the pool to itself measures the smaller half of the answer. This is independent of the rejection and applies to exp 266's stickiness and anything after it.

Losing the pool's parallelism costs a caller nothing at point-read sizes. Eight distinct point reads issued together run four-wide across four workers and strictly serially when the caller runs them itself, and serial is 70% faster, reproduced in both pairs of both collections. Four workers cannot make up a per-request overhead larger than the request. This bounds the pool's value precisely — it is worth having for results large enough that decode dominates dispatch, and it is a tax below that — and it holds whatever routing policy is eventually used to act on it.

claims.text: The `select()` isolate round trip is 6.3 us of an 8.4 us canonical 6-column point read. Measured by running the query on the calling isolate instead — same `resqlite_stmt_acquire_on`, same `decodeQuery`, no SendPort and no `Isolate.exit` — which is worth a reproduced -74.8% there, -71.0% on a 21-column point read and -35.7% on a 20-row page. Two collections of four alternating-order lane-isolated AOT passes (41 then 51 samples/lane), `ab_drift_check` REPRODUCED on every primary pair in the second collection; both control lanes return more rows than the cap admits, run byte-identical code in both arms, and read +0.1% and +3.2%. Unlike claim 264.1 the effect is flat in projection width, because what it removes is per-request rather than per-slot. The routing candidate that produced this number is REJECTED (claim 265.6); the number is not, and it is the denominator any future candidate in this direction should be compared against. Collected against 4b963ad, before exp 266's stickiness landed; exp 266's term decays to -1.6% by a statement's eight-thousandth execution and every lane here runs well past that, so the pricing should hold on current main but was not re-measured there.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · macOS 26.2 · Dart 3.12.2 · AOT CLI bundle · lane-isolated, 4 alternating-order passes x 2 collections · host at 0-39% CPU idle · pre-266 baseline · 2026-08

claims.text: Routing a `select()` to the calling isolate on the strength of a per-SQL row-count high-water mark is REJECTED, because row count cannot bound main-isolate work along three independent axes. (1) Bytes: one row can be arbitrarily large, `SELECT * FROM photos WHERE id = ?` keeps a permanent high-water mark of 1, and with no hop to serialise for, exp 236's 256 KB blob wrap is suppressed — so a 5 MB image copies straight onto the calling isolate, unchecked. Cost varies per execution of the same statement, so no per-SQL history repairs it. (2) Query cost: `count(*)` over a large table and an unindexed `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10` return few rows after unbounded work, which a result-shape signal cannot see because the work precedes the first row. (3) Scheduling: an inline `select()` returns a `List` rather than a `Future`, so a chain of them drains in microtasks with no event-loop turn — N reads are one uninterruptible block, not N interleavable slices, evidenced by exp 265's own `point1` lane at 200 reads / 427 us. The first draft of the writeup claimed a `~16 us per admitted read` bound; that was the bound for the measured shapes (small integers, short TEXT, indexed lookups, hot cache) stated as though general. Prototype preserved at `archive/exp-265`.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · analysis against the exp 265 prototype; failure modes identified by inspection, not measured — the discriminating lanes do not exist yet · 2026-08

claims.text: A read that never enters the dispatch queue is ~19x faster than one that does when the pool is busy. One point read issued while four outstanding 1,000-row reads occupy all four workers measures 533-1169 us across four passes against 37-52 us inline (-94.9% mean, REPRODUCED in both pairs). The hop's cost to a caller is its latency plus the queue depth in front of it, and every prior measurement of transfer cost in this direction held the request population constant and therefore measured only the first term. Independent of exp 265's rejection: it is a property of the queue, not of the routing policy.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · `point-under-load` lane, 4 background 1,000-row reads, 10 timed point reads/sample · 2026-08

claims.text: Serialising concurrent point reads on one isolate beats spreading them across the four-worker pool. Eight distinct point reads issued together via `Future.wait` measure -70.3% inline (REPRODUCED, both pairs, 10 groups per sample). The pool's parallelism cannot recover a per-request overhead larger than the request itself, which bounds where the pool is worth having: above the size at which decode dominates dispatch, and not below it.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · `concurrent8` lane, 8 distinct 1-row statements x 10 groups/sample · 2026-08

claims.text: An abort-and-fall-back cap costs +24.7% on the one execution that trips it, once per statement, and is the one part of exp 265's design that survives its rejection — because it enforces rather than predicts. A statement armed by two one-row executions and then returning 400 rows starts decoding inline, throws past row 64, resets and re-runs on a worker: 129 us against 163 us, REPRODUCED in both pairs. It cannot recur, because the high-water mark rises with the large result. The reset is not optional: a statement abandoned mid-iteration holds its connection's read transaction open, and every later read on that connection is then served from the pre-abort snapshot. Any future routing design should reuse this shape and add byte and VM-step caps beside it, rather than improving the predictor in front of it.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · `cap-abort` lane, fresh SQL string per sample · 2026-08

claims.text: A reader connection reserved for the calling isolate costs +0.1 to +1.7 MB of peak RSS, with two of nine lanes reading slightly down — at or below what exp 261's guard resolves (claim 261.2). Expected, since a connection's page cache is demand-filled and the inline connection reads pages the workers have already made resident. Recorded because it prices the connection for any future design that needs one: it cannot be shared with an idle worker, since the reply that frees a worker slot is sent before the worker's `finally` releases its connection, so `isAvailable` on the main isolate does not imply idle in C, and the connections are `SQLITE_OPEN_NOMUTEX`.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · maxRss, one process per lane, 9 lanes · 2026-08

nextSignals: `benchmark/experiments/select_inline_dispatch.dart` is kept as the gate for read *routing*, and its lane set is deliberately incomplete — that incompleteness is the finding. Keep `mixed6-1k` and `int20-10k`: both return more rows than any plausible cap, so they run byte-identical code in both arms and read a cross-worktree binary offset directly (the exp 254 trap). Keep `cap-abort` on a fresh SQL string per sample, since an abort is once-per-statement and any other construction leaves the lane inert after its first sample. Keep `point-under-load` and `concurrent8`, which measure admission rather than transfer. Then add the three lanes exp 265 lacked before trusting any successor: a one-row read returning a 5 MB blob, a `count(*)` over a large table, and a frame-shaped workload that can see microtask coalescing. The first two fail against `archive/exp-265`.

Any successor to exp 265 must enforce rather than predict. `sqlite3_column_bytes` reports a cell's size before it is copied into Dart, and the value is already loaded at the line where the blob-wrap branch is skipped, so a running byte cap is one comparison. `sqlite3_progress_handler` interrupts every N VM steps and bounds the cases where work precedes the first row. Neither addresses microtask coalescing — an inline read returns a `List`, not a `Future`, so it never yields — and that needs a per-drain time budget, which is a design question rather than a guard. A candidate that solves two of the three is not ready.

Exp 239 was rejected because queue depth cannot encode query cost; exp 265 because row count cannot either. The generalisation is worth stating once so a third experiment does not rediscover it: no signal derived from a query's *shape* or its *position in a queue* bounds its cost, because the expensive part can precede the first row and can hide inside one cell. The signals that do bound cost are the ones SQLite computes while running — VM steps, column bytes — and they are only available mid-flight, which forces an abort-and-retry structure rather than an admission test.

Stream reruns look like the obvious next application of inline routing and are not a shortcut around this rejection: `selectIfChanged` on an unchanged result is a C hash pass with no Dart decode, the cheapest thing the pool carries and so the largest relative hop, but an unchanged result is still produced by a query whose cost row count cannot predict. All three of claim 265.6's failure modes apply unchanged. If it is attempted, exp 249's rule holds — A/B across worktrees on `benchmark/experiments/stream_rerun_latency.dart`, never with an in-process toggle.

Exp 265's collections were taken on a host at 0-39% CPU idle with load average near 37, none of it the run's doing, which is the second consecutive experiment under claim 264.6's conditions. The order-flipped design and the two mechanically-inert controls carried it — controls at +0.1% and +3.2% against primaries of -35% to -95% — but exp 264's proposed fix still stands unbuilt: sample idle CPU at lane start and print it beside the medians, so a reader can see the host's state without taking the runner's word for it.
